Instead, you'd just have less people who are able to actually afford living expenses because they either don't have a job or don't earn enough money from working lesser hours, which then increases reliance on social programs. In the long run, this would hurt significantly businesses, because less people have disposable income. Markets wouldn't be decimated, but they shrink in the long run under a high tax system compared to a low tax system.

Illegal immigrants undercut American workers while making use of public systems -- infrastructure mainly, but in cases there are healthcare and education benefits added to the mix -- without paying any taxes aside from consumption taxes, and at the expense of legal workers. I'm all for a pathway to citizenship. Give these guys a green card and let them become fully productive members of society, but as a matter of principal, don't let them become citizens until everybody who is currently in line legally today naturalizes first. I'd say having a long waiting period to naturalize is a very reasonable punishment (I don't like using that word here because it implies vindictiveness, but can't think of a better word for it) for entering illegally and then free riding on our public goods.

4) I agree, businesses paying higher wages would mean more income tax. But if minimum wages rise and employees are fired, causing further strain on the safety nets we have in place, then the increased tax revenue is turning into nothing more than a transfer payment, which is basically useless on a macro scale without growing employment opportunities. Besides, why should we want more tax revenue? I think the government spends too much money as it is, especially given that 63% of our Federal budget goes to transfer payments. I'd rather see less tax revenue and correspondingly less government spending, which is totally feasible when less people need safety nets.

In terms of wall street corruption, which I should also extend to big business corruption in general, I think corporations should be flat out prohibited from making campaign donations. Corporations are not citizens and do not get to vote, so why should they be able to fund candidates? They could still give to super pacs, but so long as dealings between super pacs and candidates are transparent, it should be a lot more difficult for cronyism to creep into government. Cronyism from both parties lends itself to tons of government waste. So both of those suggestions wouldn't do anything to increase the size of government, but could help decrease it.

8) Solving income inequality by taxing the hell out of people isn't good policy. By comparison, growing economies also means growing competition, which allows more people to dip their hands into the GDP. There will always be income inequality, but taxing it away is inefficient.

I appreciate the thought you're putting into this and think we have similar intentions, but these are just better policies.
